page: Vultr vhf-3c-8gb is an x86_64 virtual server belonging to the High Frequency Compute family. It features 3 Intel vCPUs mapped to 3 physical cores with a shared CPU allocation and a clock speed of 2.0 GHz. The system is equipped with 8.0 GB of system memory, providing 2.67 GB of RAM per core. Local storage is bundled, consisting of a 256 GB NVMe SSD. Additionally, the instance includes one complimentary public IPv4 address.

Performance benchmarks reveal a mixed profile. The server excels in single-threaded gzip compression, placing in the top 10% with a throughput of 38.09 GB/sec. However, multi-core and memory-intensive operations show limitations. Geekbench multi-core and Passmark CPU scores fall into the bottom 25%, reflecting the shared CPU allocation. Large-block memory bandwidth is also weak, with read and write speeds of 32.54 GB/sec and 16.94 GB/sec respectively. While small-block cached memory reads are average at 395.59 GB/sec, database operations and small-model LLM inference remain in the middle tier.

Given its shared CPU architecture and bundled NVMe storage, this instance offers a resource-dense entry point for workloads that do not require sustained, dedicated CPU performance. It is well-suited for lightweight web serving, basic database operations, single-threaded file compression tasks, and development environments. It is less appropriate for heavy multi-threaded compilation, large-scale LLM inference, or memory-bound high-performance computing due to the observed performance drop-offs in those areas.

Benchmark data indicates strong single-threaded performance, notably in gzip compression, which reaches the top 10% tier at 38.09 GB/sec. However, the shared CPU allocation leads to weaker multi-core and large-block memory bandwidth results, placing Geekbench multi-core and Passmark CPU scores in the bottom 25%. This server represents a cost-efficient option for workloads requiring fast local storage and moderate compute, such as lightweight database operations, basic web serving, and single-threaded processing tasks, while avoiding sustained multi-threaded or memory-intensive applications.
